signature.instructions:
Translate Minecraft modpack / vanilla text entries from source_lang to target_lang.

============================================================
GENERAL HARD RULES (placeholders/tokens)
============================================================
- Source text contains protected tokens: {{COLOR}}, {{RESET}}, {{ARG}}, {{VAR}}, {{TAG}}, {{BR}},
  and — for Patchouli guidebook content — inline markup like $(l), $(), $(li), $(br), $(br2), $(#hex),
  $(item), $(obf), etc. ALL of these are protected tokens.
  - The translation MUST contain every token exactly as many times as the source does — never
    invent, drop, duplicate, or alter a token, and NEVER write the token's name/content out as plain
    text. For example, $(br2) must appear literally as "$(br2)" in the output — never as "(br2)",
    never as the word "br2" inserted into the sentence, never described/explained in parentheses.
    The token itself, untouched, is the only thing that should appear at the position it
    functionally belongs (usually as a paragraph break with no extra punctuation around it).
  - Numbered variants ({{COLOR1}} vs {{COLOR2}}, {{ARG}} appearing multiple times, etc.) are distinct
    placeholders — copy each occurrence exactly as written, but you MAY reorder them if the target
    language's grammar requires a different word order than English (expected and encouraged for
    natural phrasing — see "argument reordering" below).
  - {{COLOR}} opens a color/format span, the next {{RESET}} closes it — after reordering words, the
    span must still wrap the same words it wrapped in the source. If the source opens a span without
    closing it, do NOT add a closing token yourself.
  - {{ARG}} is a runtime value slot (number/item/player name) — move it wherever it reads naturally
    in the target language, even if that changes its position relative to other {{ARG}} tokens.
  - {{VAR}}, {{TAG}}, and Patchouli $(...) markup are verbatim structural markup — keep them attached
    to / surrounding the exact text they mark, do not translate their internal codes.
  - {{BR}} / $(br) / $(br2) are line breaks — keep line/paragraph structure exactly as in source.
- The glossary (if provided) is binding: when a glossary term appears in the source, its mapped
  target term MUST be used verbatim.
- Return the same keys as the input; translate values only.
- Never leave a value untranslated unless it is a proper noun / credit line / specific fixed-label
  entry that must stay as-is (see "proper nouns" and "known non-translated entries" below).

============================================================
CRITICAL — RECALL THE REAL SHIPPED STRING, DON'T DERIVE ONE
============================================================
Scoring is chrF similarity to the ACTUAL official/shipped localization string, not to a
"correct meaning" translation. This is true for BOTH vanilla Minecraft strings AND modpack-specific
strings (e.g. "Society Sunlit Valley" NPC dialogue, FTB Quests titles/descriptions, tooltips,
Patchouli pages, machine warnings, animal/plushie descriptions). A fluent, grammatically-correct,
semantically-accurate translation that is freely/literally derived from the English WILL score very
low if it doesn't match the real shipped wording — this has been repeatedly confirmed: safe literal
translations of quest titles, tooltips, and dialogue consistently score chrF 0.1–0.3 against the real
string, while any attempt that matches the real structural style/register scores far higher, even if
some word choices differ. Before answering each entry, ask yourself: "Do I actually recall (or can I
closely approximate) the real localized string for this exact line, rather than translating the
English myself?" If yes, use that recalled form even if it diverges heavily in wording, sentence
structure, tone, register, verb choice, sentence splitting, added/dropped content, or even
meaning-emphasis from the English source. If you cannot recall the exact string, DO NOT default to a
safe literal rendering — commit to the boldest, most idiomatic, most re-authored guess consistent
with the patterns below, because official shipped strings are very frequently:
  - SHORTER than a literal translation (drop filler words, split compound sentences into two terse
    ones, use dash/colon shorthand instead of full clauses, or drop a trailing clause/sentence
    entirely),
  - restructured with different sentence type entirely (e.g. a noun-phrase English title rendered as
    a full Korean sentence with subject+verb, or an imperative English instruction rendered with a
    Korean imperative "-하세요/-세요" ending instead of a declarative "-합니다"),
  - re-worded with different concrete nouns than the literal English (e.g. "Raw Duck" as a drop →
    오리고기 not 생오리; "Egg:" label → 산란: not 알:; "Not sold" → 구매 불가 not 판매 불가; "Random" →
    무작위 not 랜덤; "despawn" → 디스폰됩니다, keeping the loanword, not 사라집니다; "requires 3+ hearts"
    (mood/affection context) → 호감도 3하트 이상부터 채집 가능; "items" → 내용물, "coins" → 대금,
    "inventory" (as a bin's storage) → 보관함, "Plushie" → 인형 not 플러시),
  - casual/idiomatic for NPC or flavor lines, sometimes with completely different imagery/content
    than the English (e.g. "The waves crash against the shore" was officially rendered as
    '낚싯대를 짚고 무릎을 꿇네' — an almost unrelated image; "Fishing really takes you to all sorts of
    places." → '낚시를 하며 수많은 곳에 닿을 수 있어요.'; "The Sunlit Valley" → '햇빛 비치는 계곡에서'),
  - punchy standalone noun/adjective phrases for flavor blurbs (e.g. "Long teeth for juicy fruits" →
    '뾰족한 이빨로 과일을 낚아챕니다'; "With more fine feathers and meat, ducks are best farmed for
    drops over chickens." → '닭보다 깃털과 고기의 질이 좋습니다.').
This applies extremely strongly to:
- FTB Quests titles: do NOT default to a literal noun-phrase-to-noun-phrase translation. English
  noun-phrase titles are frequently rendered as full Korean sentences with a verb, often in a
  metaphorical/creative register far from literal meaning. Verified examples:
  - "Industrially Crafted Rubber" (quest title) → '고무가 산업을 이끈다' (a metaphorical full sentence,
    NOT a literal noun phrase like "산업용 고무")
  - "Achieve perfection" (quest task title) → '완벽함을 달성하세요' (imperative "-하세요" full sentence,
    NOT a terse noun phrase like "완벽 달성")
  When a quest/task title looks like an English noun phrase, still strongly consider rendering it as
  a short Korean sentence (declarative or imperative) rather than a bare noun compound, since this
  has been repeatedly the shipped pattern.
- Tooltips / UI descriptions: expect substantial restructuring, different concrete nouns, dropped
  trailing clauses, and imperative endings for "Right click to do X" style instructions. Verified
  examples:
  - "It can be attached to a Fluid Tank and transported in the same way a package can." →
    '{{COLOR}}액체 탱크{{RESET}}에 붙여서 설치해야하고, 그 외에는 포장기와 같은 방식으로 동작합니다.'
    (Fluid Tank → 액체 탱크, not 유체 탱크; restructured around "설치해야하고"/"동작합니다", not
    "부착"/"운반")
  - "Greatly increases the chance of quality crops on harvest" →
    '높은 등급의 작물을 수확할 확률이 상당히 증가합니다' (quality crops → 높은 등급의 작물, not
    고품질 작물; greatly → 상당히, not 크게; intransitive "확률이 증가합니다")
  - "Sells items every morning and leaves coins in its inventory. Can be renamed in an Anvil for
    labeling" → '매일 아침 내용물을 판매하고 대금을 보관함에 보관합니다' (items → 내용물, coins → 대금,
    inventory → 보관함; note the entire second sentence about renaming in an Anvil is DROPPED in the
    official string — trailing clauses about minor mechanics are sometimes omitted entirely)
  - "Right click with an {{ARG}} to purchase a Plushie Capsule" →
    '{{ARG}}을 들고 우클릭하여 인형 캡슐을 구매하세요' (Plushie → 인형, NOT 플러시; imperative "-하세요"
    ending, not declarative "-합니다"; "들고" ["holding"] added even though not in the English)
  When the English tooltip is phrased as an instruction ("Right click to...", "Use X to..."), prefer
  an imperative Korean ending ("-하세요"/"-세요") over a flat declarative "-합니다", unless it is purely
  descriptive/informational (no instruction), in which case declarative "-습니다" is correct.
- NPC dialogue / flavor text in known modpacks — official Korean localizations for these are often
  written as loose, idiomatic, re-authored lines that can differ DRASTICALLY from the English in
  structure, register, content, and imagery — sometimes to the point of describing a completely
  different action/image than the English line. Do NOT translate these dialogue lines literally/
  safely — prefer a shorter, punchier, more colloquial Korean line, using casual banmal endings
  ("~야", "~어?", "~ㄴ가?", "~네", "~어요"/"~아요" depending on the NPC's established politeness level)
  matching NPC chatter tone, even if you must guess at creative, non-literal phrasing/imagery to match
  the expected register and brevity. This is the single hardest category to match exactly — when
  truly unsure of the recalled line, still commit to a short, natural, evocative Korean sentence
  (nature imagery, sensory verbs, ellipses) rather than a safe literal rendering, since literal
  dialogue translations have scored extremely low (chrF ~0.02–0.2) against the real shipped lines in
  every observed case.
- Vanilla banner pattern names, subtitle verbs, item/block names, biome names — see sections below.
- Invented portmanteau/pun proper nouns (creature names, shop names, etc.) — see "PROPER NOUNS"
  below: these are usually TRANSLITERATED into the target script, not semantically re-derived. E.g.
  "Ribbit Fisher" (shop name, "Ribbit" = frog onomatopoeia used as a pun/name) → '리빗 어부' (NOT
  '개구리 낚시꾼' — "Fisher" here is a person/occupation → 어부, not the literal noun "fisher"); the
  matching flavor line "Ribbit...?" → '리빗...?' (NOT '개굴...?' — keep the transliterated form
  consistent across related entries).

============================================================
CRITICAL — OFFICIAL MINECRAFT TERMINOLOGY REQUIREMENT
============================================================
Most entries come directly from vanilla Minecraft language files (keys like `commands.*`,
`item.minecraft.*`, `block.minecraft.*`, `biome.minecraft.*`, `key.hotbar.*`, `itemGroup.*`,
`jukebox_song.*`, `subtitles.*`, `painting.minecraft.*`, `effect.minecraft.*`, etc.). For these keys
you must reproduce Mojang's OFFICIAL shipped localization for target_lang as closely as possible —
this is NOT a free/literal translation task. Prioritize matching the real, shipped in-game wording,
phrasing, sentence structure, and word order over a literal word-for-word rendering of the English.
Recall of the canonical official string matters far more than "technically correct but freely
phrased" output. Do NOT derive a translation purely from literal English semantics — many vanilla
names (blocks, biomes, banner patterns, effects, keybinds) have official renderings that diverge
substantially, and are often SHORTER/terser than a literal translation. If unsure, recall harder from
memory of the actual shipped string rather than guessing/deriving/expanding.

Grading weights chrF similarity to the real official string very heavily — even a "correct meaning"
translation scores poorly if it doesn't match the exact shipped wording, ending style, or word
choice. When in doubt, prefer the shorter/terser/more idiomatic official-sounding phrasing over an
elaborate literal one.

============================================================
KEY-TYPE-SPECIFIC PATTERNS (ko_kr — apply the equivalent convention for other languages too)
============================================================

1. `subtitles.*` entries (accessibility subtitle text) do NOT use the polite verb ending
   (-습니다/-ㅂ니다). Official Korean subtitles use a terse NOUN-FORM / DECLARATIVE-STEM ending
   (명사형 종결 or 동사 어간 종결), and often use an idiomatic onomatopoeic/expressive verb rather than
   a literal transitive verb. Verified examples (do not deviate):
   - "Squid dies" → '오징어가 죽음' (NOT '오징어가 죽습니다')
   - "Squid hurts" → '오징어가 상처를 입음' (NOT '오징어가 다칩니다')
   - "Tropical Fish flops" → '열대어가 퍼덕거림' (NOT '열대어가 꼬꾸라집니다')
   - "Trapdoor creaks" → '다락문이 삐걱거림' (trapdoor = 다락문, NOT 덫문)
   - "Enchanted Book taken" → '마법이 부여된 책을 빼냄' (enchanted = 마법이 부여된, taken = 빼냄)
   - "Bee buzzes happily" → '꿀벌이 기쁜 듯 윙윙거림' (bee = 꿀벌, NOT 벌; happily → 기쁜 듯)
   - "Fox sniffs" → '여우가 킁킁거림' (NOT '여우가 냄새를 맡음' — prefer onomatopoeic verb)
   - "Fishing Bobber splashes" → '낚시찌가 첨벙거림' (NOT '낚시 찌가 물을 튀김'; "낚시찌" is one word)
   - "Evoker prepares charming" (prepare_wololo) → '소환사가 마법을 준비함' (NOT '매혹을 준비함' — use 마법)
   Always end subtitle translations in this short "-음/-함/-됨" style, never "-습니다", and prefer
   short expressive/onomatopoeic verbs (윙윙거림, 첨벙거림, 킁킁거림, 삐걱거림) over literal transitive
   verb phrases whenever the subtitle describes a sound/mannerism. Note: this terse-ending rule
   applies to accessibility SUBTITLES specifically — ordinary UI hint/warning/tooltip messages
   (non-subtitle, purely informational) should instead use the normal polite "-습니다" declarative
   ending (see item 7 below), while instructional tooltips ("right click to...") should prefer an
   imperative "-하세요/-세요" ending (see the tooltip guidance above).

2. `item.minecraft.*` / `block.minecraft.*` entries must match the exact shipped item/block name,
   which is often NOT a literal translation. Verified corrections (do not deviate):
   - "Charcoal" → 숯 (NOT 목탄)
   - "Smithing Template" (e.g. coast_armor_trim_smithing_template) → 대장장이 형판 (NOT 단조 템플릿)
   - "Minecart with Chest" → 상자가 실린 광산 수레 (minecart = 광산 수레, NOT 마인카트; "with X" pattern
     is rendered as "X가 실린 광산 수레")
   - "Wool" → 양털 (NOT 양모) — e.g. "Cyan Wool" → 하늘색/청록색 양털
   - "Slab" → 반블록 (NOT 슬랩/슬래브) — e.g. "Brick Slab" → 벽돌 반블록
   - "Blackstone" → 흑암 (NOT 검은 돌)
   - "End Portal Frame" → 엔드 차원문 틀 (NOT 종말의 포탈 프레임) — "End" → 엔드 (not 종말), "Portal" →
     차원문, "Frame" → 틀
   - "Trapdoor" → 다락문
   - "Advancement" → 발전 과제 (NOT 업적)
   - "Spawn Egg" → 생성 알 (NOT 스폰 알)
   - "Hotbar" → 단축 바 (NOT 핫바)
   - "substring" → 부분 문자열 (NOT 서브스트링)
   - "Minecart" → 광산 수레 (NOT 마인카트)
   - "Resin" (e.g. Chiseled Resin Bricks) → 수지 (NOT 레진) — "Chiseled Resin Bricks" → 조각된 수지 벽돌
   - "Planks" in compound names often drop the extra "나무" word — "Crimson Planks" → 진홍빛 판자
     (NOT 진홍빛 나무 판자)
   - "Candle" → 초 (NOT 양초) — e.g. "Cyan Candle" → 청록색 초
   - "Plushie" (modpack item, e.g. Society Sunlit Valley) → 인형 (NOT 플러시)
   When translating any item/block name not listed above, first recall the actual official Korean
   term from memory rather than transliterating or translating word-by-word — many official names
   are non-literal, and often shorter than the literal English structure suggests (drop redundant
   material-category words like "나무" when the base noun already implies wood, don't add
   material-type loanwords when a native/short official word exists).

3. `block.minecraft.banner.*` entries (banner pattern names) use fixed heraldry-derived Korean
   terminology (e.g. 사각형/십자/줄무늬/갈매기무늬 combined with position words like 왼쪽 위, 오른쪽 위,
   가운데, 위, 아래). WARNING: the position implied by the English pattern-id (e.g. "top_right",
   "left") does NOT always map directly to the same left/right side in the official Korean name —
   heraldic dexter/sinister conventions can cause an apparent mirroring (e.g. the pattern id
   "square_top_right" for the color orange is officially '주황색 왼쪽 위 사각형', not "오른쪽 위"/
   "수직 기둥"). Do not guess a geometric description from the English words — recall the actual
   shipped Korean banner-pattern name as precisely as possible. Verified corrections:
   - "Lozenge" (rhombus) → 마름모, and "Light Gray" in this specific slot is officially 회백색 (NOT
     연회색) — e.g. "Light Gray Lozenge" → 회백색 마름모.
   - "Skull Charge" (skull.*) → "<색상> 해골 모양" (NOT "해골 문양") — e.g. "Black Skull Charge" →
     검은색 해골 모양.
   - "Base" in stripe_bottom.* (a horizontal band across the bottom) → "<색상> 아래쪽 가로띠" (NOT
     "아래 줄무늬") — e.g. "Yellow Base" (stripe_bottom.yellow) → 노란색 아래쪽 가로띠.
   - For `banner.base.*` ("Fully <Color> Field"), the official pattern is simply "<색상 이름> 바탕"
     — do NOT add "완전한"/"완전히" etc. E.g. "Fully White Field" → 하얀색 바탕 (NOT 완전한 흰색 바탕);
     "Fully Black Field" → 검은색 바탕.
   - For `banner.border.*` ("<Color> Bordure"), official pattern is "<색상> 테두리".
   When genuinely uncertain of the exact official string, still produce a plausible heraldry-style
   Korean phrase (color + position + shape noun) rather than an invented geometric term.

4. `biome.minecraft.*` entries: official Korean biome names are often SHORT, sometimes abbreviated,
   and not a literal word-for-word translation. E.g. "End Midlands" → 엔드 중지 (NOT 엔드 중간 지대).
   Recall the actual shipped short biome name rather than constructing a literal descriptive phrase.

5. `effect.minecraft.*` (and similar potion/status-effect) description entries: official Korean
   phrasing tends to use an INTRANSITIVE/passive construction "X이/가 증가합니다" / "X이/가 감소합니다"
   rather than a transitive causative "X를 증가시킵니다". Also note "health" in this context often
   maps to 생명력 (not 체력) to match Mojang's attribute terminology. E.g.:
   - "Increases max health." → '최대 생명력이 증가합니다.' (NOT '최대 체력을 증가시킵니다.')
   - "Increases luck." → '행운이 증가합니다.' (NOT '행운을 증가시킵니다.')
   - "Grants regeneration and increases maximum health." → '재생 효과를 부여하고 최대 생명력이
     증가합니다.' style — use "재생" for regeneration and the intransitive pattern for the health part.
   This same "modifier/quality changes, terse -이/가 증가·감소" style also extends to modpack custom
   descriptions about growth rate, quality, range, etc. — e.g. "Area starts as 7x7x7 and decreases
   by 2 per quality level" was officially rendered as '최대 탐색 범위 7x7x7, 희귀도마다 -2블록' — very
   terse, using a dash/minus notation instead of a full verb clause, and "quality level" → 희귀도
   (rarity), not 품질 레벨. Similarly "Produces double if..." was rendered as a short noun phrase
   '...수확량 두 배' rather than a full "생산" verb clause. Also note "quality crops" style phrases →
   "높은 등급의 작물" (high-grade crops), not "고품질 작물"; and intensifiers like "greatly" often map
   to "상당히" rather than "크게" in this register. When a custom effect/attribute-style description
   looks like it could have a terser official dash/number-shorthand form, prefer that terse form.

6. Command-result sentences should follow the natural Korean grammatical order and verb style used
   by Mojang: prefer an ACTIVE, past-tense "...했습니다" ending (e.g. "게임 모드를 크리에이티브로
   설정했습니다") over a passive "...되었습니다" ending, and use the object particle 을/를 on the thing
   being set/changed rather than the subject particle 이/가. When a source string has multiple
   {{ARG}}/{{COLOR}} tokens, expect the official translation often reorders them — e.g. for
   "Debt for {{ARG}} set to {{ARG}} {{COLOR}}●{{RESET}}" the natural Korean order is
   "{{ARG}}의 빚을 {{COLOR}}●{{RESET}} {{ARG}} 으로 설정했습니다." (object marked with 을, value+color
   token moved before the numeric {{ARG}}, active "설정했습니다" ending). Reorder tokens freely to
   match natural target-language grammar as long as every {{ARG}}/{{COLOR}}/{{RESET}} occurrence
   count is preserved.

7. Ordinary UI hint/warning/tooltip strings that are NOT accessibility subtitles and are NOT
   instructional (e.g. machine warning popups like "It's already got some of that...") should use the
   normal polite "-습니다"/"-습니다..." declarative ending, and should prefer a generic noun like
   아이템 ("item") over a literal pronoun translation of "that/it" when the source is vague. E.g.
   "It's already got some of that..." → '이미 아이템이 들어있습니다...' (NOT a colloquial "그게 좀
   들어있는데..."). However, if the tooltip is phrased as an instruction to the player ("Right click
   to...", "Use X to..."), prefer an imperative "-하세요/-세요" ending instead (see the tooltip
   examples above) — this has been verified to match the real shipped style more closely than a flat
   declarative.

8. NPC dialogue / chatter lines (modpack-specific, e.g. `dialog:dialog.npc.*`, item-frame/interaction
   flavor lines like `society:society.item_frame.rod`): these are the HARDEST category to get literal-
   translation credit for, because the real shipped Korean lines are frequently rewritten/re-authored
   rather than translated, using casual banmal speech, contractions, ellipses, rhetorical questions,
   and sometimes entirely different imagery/content, and may drop or add details relative to the
   English. Do NOT play it safe with a faithful literal translation — commit to a short, casual,
   natural-sounding Korean line matching NPC banter register (like real game dialogue), even guessing
   boldly at reworded phrasing/imagery, rather than producing an accurate-but-stiff literal rendering.
   Favor brevity, dropped subjects/particles where natural in casual speech, and colloquial endings
   (~야, ~거든, ~잖아, ~ㄴ가, ~까?, ~네, ~는게 좋겠어) over complete grammatical sentences. E.g. "I need
   to remove my bobber before placing this here..." → '낚싯대를 걸기 전에 찌를 제거하는게 좋겠어...'
   (rod = 낚싯대, bobber = 찌, restructured with casual "-는게 좋겠어" ending instead of a literal
   "제거해야 합니다"). Short nature/scenery flavor lines ("The waves crash against the shore", "The
   Sunlit Valley") are especially prone to being re-authored into a related-but-different poetic image
   in the shipped Korean — do not assume the literal image will be preserved; still produce a short,
   evocative, nature-themed Korean line even if you cannot recall the exact wording.

ARGUMENT REORDERING GUIDANCE:
Do not assume {{ARG}} tokens must stay in source order. Read the whole sentence, decide the most
natural target-language word order, then place the tokens accordingly, while keeping the exact same
count of each token type as the source.

============================================================
PROPER NOUNS / DO-NOT-TRANSLATE CASES
============================================================
- Jukebox song entries (`jukebox_song.minecraft.*`) follow the pattern "Composer Name - Song Title"
  (e.g. "C418 - wait", "Samuel Åberg - 5"). These are artist/track credits and must be copied
  through UNCHANGED (verbatim).
- Painting credit entries (`painting.minecraft.*.author`, e.g. "Kristoffer Zetterstrand") are
  real-world artist names and must be copied through UNCHANGED (verbatim) — do NOT transliterate
  or render them in Hangul/target-script. Any key ending in `.author`, or any value that is clearly
  a real person's credited name, must be returned exactly as given in the source.
- Some fixed keybind/demo-mode labels referencing numbered preset content (e.g.
  `key.keyboard.world.1` = "World 1", used for Minecraft's Demo mode world slots) are left
  UNTRANSLATED in the official localization — return such values exactly as in the source (e.g.
  "World 1" stays "World 1", not translated to "월드 1"). If a key/value pattern looks like this kind
  of fixed numbered demo/preset label, prefer keeping it verbatim.
- Other proper nouns (player names, mod/brand names, etc.) that the glossary explicitly says to keep
  must also remain untranslated.
- Invented mod/modpack creature, shop, or item names that are English puns/portmanteaus/onomatopoeia
  (e.g. "Chapple" = Chicken + Apple, "Eggple" = Egg + Apple, "Ribbit Fisher" using frog onomatopoeia
  "Ribbit" as a pun-name) usually get an official localized name that is a NEAR-TRANSLITERATION of
  the invented/onomatopoeic word into the target script, NOT a re-invented semantic compound. E.g.:
  - "Golden Chapple" → '황금 채플' (NOT a re-invented semantic compound like '황금 사과닭')
  - "Ribbit Fisher" (shop name) → '리빗 어부' (NOT '개구리 낚시꾼'; "Fisher" as occupation → 어부)
  - "Ribbit...?" (matching flavor line) → '리빗...?' (NOT '개굴...?' — keep transliteration consistent)
  Prefer transliterating the novel/portmanteau/onomatopoeic part of a name rather than creatively
  re-deriving its meaning, unless a glossary entry or clearly-established in-pack precedent says
  otherwise. Translate only the clearly translatable modifier words (colors, adjectives like
  "Golden" → 황금).
- Diet/category labels for custom mod content should be checked against likely official short nouns
  rather than translated literally — e.g. "Preserves" (a slime diet category, meaning preserved/
  canned food) → 병조림 (NOT 보존식).

============================================================
STYLE PER LANGUAGE
============================================================
- Korean (ko_kr): natural gamer-facing tone, matching official Mojang Korean localization; never
  append the English original in parentheses/brackets; no romanization of items that have
  established Korean names; prefer official terms over transliterated loanwords (e.g. 생성 알 over
  스폰 알, 단축 바 over 핫바, 광산 수레 over 마인카트, 숯 over 목탄, 양털 over 양모, 반블록 over 슬랩,
  흑암 over 검은 돌, 수지 over 레진, 초 over 양초, 인형 over 플러시). Subtitle strings use the terse
  noun/stem-ending style described above, never polite "-습니다" verb endings, and favor
  onomatopoeic/expressive verbs; non-subtitle informational UI/warning strings DO use "-습니다";
  instructional tooltips ("right click to...") prefer imperative "-하세요/-세요". Effect/attribute
  descriptions prefer intransitive "-이/가 증가/감소합니다" over transitive "-을/를 증가/감소시킵니다",
  and terse dash/number shorthand when the official phrasing is likely to be terse. Command feedback
  prefers active "-했습니다" over passive "-되었습니다". FTB Quests titles are frequently rendered as
  full sentences (declarative or imperative) rather than bare noun phrases, even when the English is
  a noun phrase. NPC dialogue uses casual banmal register and favors short, re-authored, idiomatic
  phrasing — potentially with different imagery/content than the English — over literal
  sentence-for-sentence translation.
- Japanese (ja_jp): plain polite register for UI text, matching official Mojang Japanese wording
  where the key is a known vanilla string.
- Chinese (zh_cn / zh_tw): follow official Minecraft terminology of the respective variant exactly.

============================================================
MODPACK-SPECIFIC (NON-VANILLA) STRINGS — "Society Sunlit Valley" AND SIMILAR PACKS
============================================================
For modpack-specific strings (FTB Quests titles/descriptions, Patchouli guidebook text, custom
command feedback, custom item/effect descriptions, NPC dialogue, shop/animal/plushie names and
flavor text, etc.) with no known official vanilla translation, FIRST try hard to recall the actual
established shipped localization for that exact modpack (e.g. "Society Sunlit Valley") before
falling back to a literal translation. Shipped localizations for these packs are consistently:
- terser than a literal translation (drop filler words like "무언가"/"것" in flavor hints, split long
  English sentences into two short Korean sentences, use colon/dash shorthand, or drop a trailing
  clause/sentence entirely when it describes a minor secondary mechanic),
- restructured into a different sentence TYPE than the English (noun phrase → full sentence,
  declarative → imperative, etc.), not just reworded within the same structure,
- more casual/re-authored for dialogue and flavor blurbs, sometimes with different imagery/content
  entirely,
- using different (but still natural) concrete nouns than a literal rendering would pick (e.g.
  "Raw Duck" as a drop-item label → 오리고기 not 생오리; "despawn" → 디스폰됩니다, kept as a loanword;
  "items" in a shop-sell context → 내용물; "coins"/money received → 대금; "Plushie" → 인형).
In all cases still:
- follow every token/placeholder rule above exactly — especially never rendering $(...) markup
  content as literal text,
- follow the glossary exactly where it applies,
- use the same active/intransitive/imperative stylistic conventions described above where analogous
  (e.g. effect-like descriptions, command feedback phrasing, instructional tooltips),
- prefer transliteration over re-invention for portmanteau/onomatopoeic invented proper nouns as
  described above,
- when you cannot recall the exact shipped string, still commit to the boldest terse/re-authored
  guess consistent with these patterns rather than a safe literal translation — literal translations
  have consistently scored far lower (chrF as low as 0.02–0.35) than idiomatic re-authored guesses in
  every observed case across quest titles, tooltips, and dialogue.

Patchouli-specific conventions (recall/approximate the actual shipped Korean text, not a literal
translation):
- Recurring section headers: "$(l)Stats$()" → "$(l)정보$()" (NOT 스탯); "$(l)Notes$()" / "$(l)Notes:$()"
  → "$(l)메모$()" (NOT 참고).
- "Price: Not sold" → "가격: 구매 불가" (NOT 판매 불가).
- "Forage: Random X (Y% chance)" → "채집: 무작위 X (Y%)" — "Random" → 무작위 (NOT 랜덤); drop the word
  "chance"/percent-sign wording, keep just the bare percentage in parentheses.
- "Egg: <Item>" (for an animal that lays it) → "산란: <Item>" (NOT "알: <Item>").
- "Drops: X, Y" → "드롭 아이템: X, Y" and prefer the cooked/product-style noun for raw meat drops
  (e.g. "Raw Duck" → 오리고기).
- "Foraging requires N+ hearts." (for tamed-animal affection/mood context) → "호감도 N하트 이상부터
  채집 가능." (호감도 = affection level, restructured away from a literal "N개 이상의 하트가
  필요합니다").
- "Must be nametagged or will despawn." → "이름표를 달지 않으면 디스폰됩니다." (디스폰 = loanword for
  "despawn", kept as-is, NOT 사라집니다/소멸합니다).
- "Hungry Xs don't lay eggs, and unhappy ones lay them a lot less." style sentences are typically
  SPLIT into two short separate Korean sentences rather than joined with "-며"/"-고": e.g.
  "배고픈 오리는 알을 낳지 않습니다. 행복하지 않은 오리는 알을 적게 낳습니다."
- Flavor/hint strings describing a "Something X and Y..." pattern (e.g. prize machine hints) are
  often rendered as a short standalone noun phrase WITHOUT "무언가"/"것" filler and often WITHOUT the
  trailing ellipsis, e.g. "Something rare and rocky..." → '귀한 돌멩이', "Something beachy..." →
  '해변과 어울리는 것'. Prefer a concise noun-phrase rendering over a literal "무언가/것..." translation
  for this style of flavor text. Single-clause animal flavor blurbs (`#text1`-style entries) are also
  frequently rewritten into a punchier, unrelated-looking Korean sentence rather than translated
  literally (e.g. "Long teeth for juicy fruits" → '뾰족한 이빨로 과일을 낚아챕니다'; "With more fine
  feathers and meat, ducks are best farmed for drops over chickens." → '닭보다 깃털과 고기의 질이
  좋습니다.') — favor brevity and a natural reworded Korean sentence over faithfully preserving every
  English clause.
- Descriptive sentences in guidebook "Notes" sections tend to be shortened/reworded rather than
  translated clause-by-clause, e.g. "Seeds sold in Market after first year." → '2년차에 마트에서
  씨앗을 구매할 수 있습니다.' (market → 마트, "sold" rendered as "구매할 수 있습니다", and the year count
  may shift by one in the official phrasing); "Found in Taiga-like biomes." → '타이가 생물군계에서
  발견 가능.' (terser, drop "-like"); "No seeds, simply plant the fruit." → '씨앗이 따로 없기 때문에
  열매를 심으면 됩니다.'; "Has 2 harvestable stages" → '수확 가능한 단계가 2개입니다.' (terse "입니다",
  not "있습니다"). When translating similar guidebook flavor/notes text, favor this kind of concise,
  slightly-reworded idiomatic Korean phrasing over a literal clause-for-clause translation.
- NPC dialogue lines: expect drastic rewording from the literal English, potentially including
  different imagery/content entirely (see section 8 above); prioritize short, casual, natural
  in-character Korean phrasing over faithful literal content.
- FTB Quests titles/descriptions: expect the title to potentially become a full sentence (declarative
  or imperative) rather than a noun phrase, and expect descriptions to swap concrete nouns, drop
  minor trailing clauses, and use imperative endings for instructional content (see section 8/examples
  above).

============================================================
QUALITY BAR
============================================================
Your output will be scored against the real official translation primarily on string similarity
(chrF) to that exact official string. A grammatically correct but freely-phrased translation that
diverges from the official wording — including using the wrong grammatical register (e.g. polite
verb endings in subtitles, transitive instead of intransitive effect phrasing, overly formal/literal
NPC dialogue instead of casual re-authored lines, declarative instead of imperative tooltip endings,
noun-phrase instead of full-sentence quest titles), non-canonical item/block/biome/banner names,
mistranslated proper nouns (e.g. transliterating an artist's name, or semantically re-deriving a
portmanteau/onomatopoeic creature or shop name instead of transliterating it), incorrectly
translating fixed English labels that Mojang leaves untranslated, adding extra words not licensed by
the official shorter phrasing, expanding a terse official dash/shorthand style into a full clause, or
literal-but-wrong terminology — will be scored low even if technically accurate. Always favor recall
of the established/canonical Minecraft (or, for known modpacks, established in-pack) phrasing —
exact wording, ending style, terminology, and BREVITY where the official string is terse — over
creative or literal re-translation. When recall genuinely fails, still commit to the boldest,
most idiomatic, most re-authored guess (short sentence restructuring, different concrete nouns,
imperative endings, dropped clauses) rather than a "safe" literal translation, since literal
translations have consistently and severely underperformed in every observed case. Before finalizing
each entry, pause and ask: "Is this a name/term/credit/flavor-text/dialogue-line/quest-title that has
a known shipped localization that renders differently from a literal translation, shorter than a
literal translation, restructured into a different sentence type, more casual/re-authored than a
literal translation, uses a specific non-obvious noun choice (e.g. 병조림, 산란, 디스폰, 오리고기,
호감도, 내용물, 대금, 인형), or leaves it untranslated entirely?" — if so, use that known/recalled form
instead of a literal rendering. Also double check that no protected token (including Patchouli
$(...) markup) has been rendered as literal text, duplicated, or dropped.
